referents.label: LUCA, the Last Universal Common Ancestor

claims.statement: Lead isotopes in meteorites and in ocean sediment converge on an Earth about 4.55 billion years old.

status_timeline.source: Patterson 1956, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta — first isochron age for Earth and meteorites together
radiometric consensus, 1970s — independent chronometers repeatedly reproduce ~4.5 Ga; no serious rival

claims.statement: Hafnium-tungsten dating puts the end of Earth's main accretion some tens of millions of years after the Sun.
claims.asserted_by: Hf–W isotope chronology, diffuse consensus 2000s–2010s (no single originating paper)

status_timeline.source: Hf–W core-formation chronometry, early 2000s — deliberately vague; the result emerged across several groups, not one paper
cosmochemical consensus, 2010s — core formation and last giant impact separated from CAI formation by 30–100 Myr

claims.statement: The Moon condensed from debris blasted into orbit when a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth off-centre.

status_timeline.source: Hartmann & Davis 1975, Icarus — giant impact offered as one of four rival lunar-origin models
Conference on the Origin of the Moon, Kona 1984 — giant impact wins the field by elimination, but without simulations
Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature — hydrodynamic simulations finally reproduce the Moon's mass, iron deficit and angular momentum

claims.statement: Simulations show an impactor near a tenth of Earth's mass gives the right mass, spin and iron budget for the Moon.

status_timeline.source: Canup & Asphaug 2001, Nature — the canonical low-velocity, grazing giant impact
isotopic-crisis literature, early 2010s — the canonical impact makes a Moon built mostly of Theia, contradicting identical O and Ti isotopes

claims.statement: Hafnium in Apollo zircons dates the Moon's formation to 4.51 billion years ago, within 60 Myr of the Sun.

status_timeline.source: Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances — Hf model ages on eight Apollo 14 zircon fragments
lunar chronology debate, ~2020 — an early Moon conflicts with Hf–W model ages that favour a later impact

claims.statement: Tungsten model ages push the giant impact later, nearer 4.45 Ga, roughly 100 Myr after the solar system began.
claims.asserted_by: Hf–W lunar model-age literature, 2000s–2010s (diffuse; deliberately not pinned to one paper)

status_timeline.source: Hf–W lunar chronometry, mid-2000s — vague by design; several groups report ages in the 4.42–4.48 Ga range
Barboni et al. 2017, Science Advances — zircon Hf ages argue for an impact ~60 Myr earlier

claims.statement: Apollo highland rocks cluster near 3.9 Ga, read as a brief cataclysmic spike of impacts on Moon and Earth.
claims.asserted_by: Tera, Papanastassiou & Wasserburg 1974, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

status_timeline.source: Tera, Papanastassiou & Wasserburg 1974, EPSL — isotopic evidence for a terminal lunar cataclysm
Gomes, Levison, Tsiganis & Morbidelli 2005, Nature — the Nice model supplies a dynamical cause and the LHB becomes textbook
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — the age cluster may be a sampling artifact, not an impact spike

claims.statement: The 3.9 Ga age cluster may be an artifact of sampling Imbrium ejecta rather than a real bombardment spike.

status_timeline.source: Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — 'Illusory late heavy bombardments'; a monotonic decline reproduces the same age histogram
sample-bias literature, late 2010s — several groups agree the cataclysm is unproven; a milder declining flux is now widely preferred

claims.statement: Migration of Jupiter and Saturn through a resonance destabilised the outer belt and rained debris on the inner planets.

status_timeline.source: Gomes, Levison, Tsiganis & Morbidelli 2005, Nature — planetary migration as the trigger for a cataclysmic bombardment
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — if there was no spike, the model explains something that never happened

claims.statement: Ocean-boiling impacts could have repeatedly sterilised the surface, delaying or resetting the start of life.

status_timeline.source: Maher & Stevenson 1988, Nature — 'Impact frustration of the origin of life'
Boehnke & Harrison 2016, PNAS — with no cataclysm, the sterilisation window largely dissolves

claims.statement: A 4.404-billion-year-old Jack Hills zircon carries oxygen isotopes implying crust already altered by liquid water.

status_timeline.source: Wilde, Valley, Peck & Graham 2001, Nature — oldest known terrestrial mineral; a cool, wet Hadean
Hadean zircon debate, mid-2000s — critics argued the heavy δ18O could reflect later alteration or radiogenic Pb mobility
Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience — atom-probe tomography confirms the age and closes the main objection

claims.statement: Atom-probe imaging of lead clusters inside the grain shows the Hadean age is real, not a disturbed artifact.

status_timeline.source: Valley et al. 2014, Nature Geoscience — nanoscale Pb clustering dated at 3.4 Ga, leaving the 4.4 Ga crystallisation intact
Hadean geochronology consensus, late 2010s — the 4.4 Ga Jack Hills age is no longer seriously disputed

claims.statement: A liquid hydrosphere by 4.4 Ga removes the main obstacle to life having started in the Hadean.

status_timeline.source: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS — a habitable Hadean surface argued from zircon evidence
Hadean habitability literature, ~2020 — the 'cool early Earth' is broadly accepted even by those who reject Hadean life

claims.statement: Carbon-rich filaments in the 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert were described as cyanobacteria-like microfossils.

status_timeline.source: Schopf 1993, Science — eleven taxa of filamentous microfossils from the Apex chert, Pilbara
palaeontological textbook consensus, mid-1990s — the Apex filaments become the standard 'oldest fossils' in teaching and museums
Brasier et al. 2002, Nature — the filaments reinterpreted as abiogenic graphite in a hydrothermal vein
Schopf & Kudryavtsev, mid-2010s — Raman and isotope rebuttals published; the field remains split rather than resolved

claims.statement: The Apex 'microfossils' are more likely abiogenic graphite artifacts from a hot-spring vein, not fossil cells.

status_timeline.source: Brasier et al. 2002, Nature — 'Questioning the evidence for Earth's oldest fossils'
biogenicity debate, ~2010s — neither side concedes; the Apex case becomes the standard cautionary tale for biosignatures

claims.statement: A 3.43-billion-year-old reef of layered stromatolites in the Pilbara gives ecosystem-scale evidence of early life.
claims.asserted_by: Allwood, Walter, Kamber, Marshall & Burch 2006, Nature

status_timeline.source: Allwood et al. 2006, Nature — Strelley Pool Chert stromatolite reef; morphological variety argues against an abiotic origin
Allwood et al. 2009, PNAS — environmental controls on stromatolite form; now the most widely accepted Archean biosignature

claims.statement: Cone-shaped layered structures in 3.7-billion-year-old Greenland rocks were read as the oldest stromatolites.
claims.asserted_by: Nutman, Bennett, Friend, Van Kranendonk & Chivas 2016, Nature

status_timeline.source: Nutman et al. 2016, Nature — 3,700 Myr-old stromatolites newly exposed by snowmelt at Isua
Allwood et al. 2018, Nature — independent analysis finds deformation structures, no biological signal
Nutman et al. 2021 rebuttal — argues the tested sample came from an atypically deformed outcrop edge; unresolved

claims.statement: Re-examined in three dimensions, the Isua cones are deformation ridges whose chemistry carries no biological signal.
claims.asserted_by: Allwood, Rosing, Flannery, Hurowitz & Heirwegh 2018, Nature

status_timeline.source: Allwood et al. 2018, Nature — 'Reassessing evidence of life in 3,700-million-year-old rocks of Greenland'
Nutman and colleagues respond in support of the relict stromatolites; the community remains divided

claims.statement: Haematite tubes in Quebec vent rocks, at least 3.77 and perhaps 4.28 Ga old, are read as fossil vent microbes.

status_timeline.source: Dodd et al. 2017, Nature — micrometre haematite filaments in Nuvvuagittuq banded iron formation
biosignature-scepticism literature, late 2010s — abiotic haematite filaments are known, and the host rock's age itself spans 3.77–4.28 Ga

claims.statement: Graphite sealed inside a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon carries a light carbon signature that could be biological.

status_timeline.source: Bell, Boehnke, Harrison & Mao 2015, PNAS — one graphite-bearing grain out of 10,000; δ13C of −24‰, framed only as 'potentially biogenic'
isotope-scepticism literature, late 2010s — abiotic carbon can reach −24‰; a single grain cannot carry the claim. Never consensus.

claims.statement: Ribosomal RNA from every cell traces back to one shared ancestral population, split into three primary lineages.

status_timeline.source: Woese & Fox 1977, PNAS — the primary kingdoms; a universal molecular tree with a single root
microbiological resistance, ~1980 — the archaeal domain and the single-ancestor rooting were both widely rejected at first
genomic-era consensus, mid-1990s — whole-genome sequencing vindicates the three-domain rRNA tree and a universal ancestor

claims.statement: Molecular clocks on gene families that duplicated before LUCA place it around 4.2 billion years ago.
claims.asserted_by: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

status_timeline.source: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — calibrated clocks on five universal paralog trees give 4.09–4.32 Ga

claims.statement: Older molecular-clock studies spread LUCA anywhere from 3.5 to 4.5 Ga, a band wider than most fossil disputes.
claims.asserted_by: molecular-clock literature, 1990s–2010s (deliberately vague; the estimates never converged)

status_timeline.source: early universal molecular clocks, 1990s — honest vagueness: dozens of incompatible estimates, no single canonical paper
Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — a properly calibrated relaxed clock narrows the range considerably

claims.statement: LUCA looks like an anaerobic, hydrogen-using autotroph at home in a hydrothermal vent, not a generalist.

status_timeline.source: Weiss et al. 2016, Nature Microbiology — 355 gene families reconstruct a thermophilic, H2-dependent, N2-fixing LUCA
Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — reconstructs a far larger ~2,500-gene LUCA, a complex acetogen inside an existing ecosystem

claims.statement: Life's origin preceded LUCA by an unknown span: LUCA was already a complex cell embedded in an ecosystem.
claims.asserted_by: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

status_timeline.source: Moody et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution — LUCA's inferred metabolism implies recycling partners, so it was not the first cell

claims.statement: Steranes and 2-methylhopanes in 2.7-billion-year-old Pilbara shales were taken as cyanobacterial and eukaryote traces.

status_timeline.source: Brocks, Logan, Buick & Summons 1999, Science — Archean molecular fossils push oxygenic photosynthesis back 300 Myr before the GOE
biomarker consensus, early 2000s — the 'whiff of oxygen' 2.7 Ga becomes a standard fixture of early-Earth reviews
Rasmussen, Fletcher, Brocks & Kilburn 2008, Nature — the biomarkers are younger contaminants, not indigenous

claims.statement: Those Archean biomarkers were drilling contamination; ultraclean cores from the same rocks yield no steranes at all.

status_timeline.source: Rasmussen et al. 2008, Nature — carbon isotopes of the hydrocarbons clash with coexisting kerogen
French et al. 2015, PNAS — ultraclean redrilling finds no steranes; Brocks himself co-authored the retraction of the interpretation

claims.statement: Oxygenic photosynthesis may have evolved only shortly before 2.4 Ga, with oxygen then accumulating almost at once.

status_timeline.source: Kopp, Kirschvink, Hilburn & Nash 2005, PNAS — cyanobacteria radiate just before the Makganyene snowball, not hundreds of Myr earlier
oxygenation debate, 2010s — trace-metal and Mn-oxidation proxies still argue for oxygenic photosynthesis well before 2.5 Ga

claims.statement: Cyanobacterial oxygen destroyed the methane greenhouse and pushed free oxygen permanently into the air.

status_timeline.source: Kopp et al. 2005, PNAS — oxygen as a planetary poison that could flip climate in as little as 1 Myr
Lyons, Reinhard & Planavsky 2014, Nature — biological oxygen production as the driver of the GOE is not seriously disputed

claims.statement: Atmospheric oxygen first rose between 2.45 and 2.32 billion years ago, bracketed by South African redbeds.

status_timeline.source: Bekker et al. 2004, Nature — 'Dating the rise of atmospheric oxygen' pins the transition in the Transvaal and Huronian successions
Lyons, Reinhard & Planavsky 2014, Nature — the 2.45–2.32 Ga window becomes the standard GOE interval
Poulton et al. 2021, Nature — oxygen fluctuated for another 200 Myr before becoming permanent

claims.statement: Mass-independent sulfur fractionation disappears after ~2.4 Ga, the sharpest fingerprint of an oxygenating sky.

status_timeline.source: Farquhar, Bao & Thiemens 2000, Science — anomalous S-33 in Archean sulfides requires an ozone-free, oxygen-free atmosphere
Pavlov & Kasting 2002, Astrobiology — photochemical modelling ties the signal quantitatively to sub-ppm oxygen; now the GOE's smoking gun

claims.statement: Oxygen did not simply stay up: permanent atmospheric oxygenation was delayed by ~200 Myr, to about 2.22 Ga.

status_timeline.source: Poulton et al. 2021, Nature — sulfur isotopes in South African drill core show the MIF signal returning repeatedly after 2.45 Ga
oxygenation-timing literature, 2020s — a stepped, oscillating GOE is gaining ground but the endpoint is still argued

claims.statement: Free oxygen made sterol synthesis and aerobic respiration possible, opening the way to the eukaryotic cell.
claims.asserted_by: geobiological consensus since the 1970s; no single originating paper (sterol biosynthesis requires molecular oxygen)

status_timeline.source: early geobiology, ~1970 — honest vagueness: the oxygen-prerequisite argument accreted across many authors rather than one paper
geobiological consensus, ~2000 — the oxygen threshold for eukaryotes is standard, though the causal tightness is still argued
eukaryogenesis debate, late 2010s — anaerobic Asgard-archaea models weaken oxygen's role as the trigger rather than a permission

claims.statement: As oxygen rose the methane greenhouse collapsed, plunging Earth into the Makganyene snowball around 2.3 Ga.

status_timeline.source: Kopp et al. 2005, PNAS — the Paleoproterozoic snowball as a climate disaster caused by life itself
Paleoproterozoic glaciation literature, 2010s — the methane-collapse mechanism is popular but the ordering of oxygen and ice is still disputed

claims.statement: Coiled carbon ribbons in 2.1-billion-year-old Michigan iron formation are read as the oldest large eukaryotic algae.

status_timeline.source: Han & Runnegar 1992, Science — Grypania spiralis from the Negaunee Iron-Formation, 700–1000 Myr older than any prior site
Proterozoic palaeobiology debate, 2000s — Grypania's eukaryotic affinity rests on size alone; a giant bacterium is not excluded

claims.statement: Bangiomorpha, a 1.2-billion-year-old red alga from Arctic Canada, is the oldest fossil assignable to a living group.

status_timeline.source: Butterfield 2000, Paleobiology — Bangiomorpha pubescens; also the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction
Proterozoic palaeobiology consensus, 2010s — the taxonomic assignment is widely accepted, though the 1.2 Ga age has since been re-argued

claims.statement: Mitochondria and plastids are domesticated bacteria that were engulfed and kept, not organelles built from scratch.

status_timeline.source: Sagan (Margulis) 1967, Journal of Theoretical Biology — 'On the origin of mitosing cells', rejected by many journals before publication
cell-biology resistance, 1970s — the idea was treated as fringe for roughly a decade after publication
Gray & Doolittle 1982, Microbiological Reviews — organellar rRNA sequencing settles the question for mitochondria and plastids

claims.statement: Palaeomagnetism puts Neoproterozoic glacial deposits at the equator, implying the entire ocean froze over.
claims.asserted_by: Kirschvink 1992, in The Proterozoic Biosphere (Cambridge University Press)

status_timeline.source: Kirschvink 1992, The Proterozoic Biosphere — a two-page chapter that coins the term 'snowball Earth' and is largely ignored for six years
Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science — the idea is amplified into a full hypothesis and immediately attacked
Rooney, Strauss, Brandon & Macdonald 2015, Geology — synchronous long-lived global glaciations confirmed; broad but not universal acceptance

claims.statement: Namibian cap carbonates and a collapse in carbon isotopes record a global freeze ending in an extreme greenhouse.

status_timeline.source: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson & Schrag 1998, Science — 'A Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth'; CO2 rising to ~350x modern ends the freeze
Hyde, Crowley, Baum & Peltier 2000, Nature — a 'slushball' with an open tropical ocean fits the models at least as well
Rooney et al. 2015, Geology — Re–Os ages show two long, globally synchronous glaciations, hard to explain without near-total ice

claims.statement: Coupled climate-ice models make equatorial ice with an open tropical sea: a slushball rather than a snowball.

status_timeline.source: Hyde, Crowley, Baum & Peltier 2000, Nature — a refuge for photosynthetic life that a hard snowball would have killed
snowball modelling debate, 2000s–2010s — the slushball survives as a minority position; sea-glass and refugia arguments blunt its main advantage

claims.statement: Rhenium-osmium ages run the Sturtian glaciation from 717 to 661 Ma, synchronous across three palaeocontinents.

status_timeline.source: Rooney, Strauss, Brandon & Macdonald 2015, Geology — 'A Cryogenian chronology: two long-lasting synchronous Neoproterozoic glaciations'
Cryogenian geochronology consensus, ~2020 — a 56-Myr Sturtian and a short Marinoan ending at 635 Ma are now standard

claims.statement: The freeze-thaw shock and the oxygen pulse that followed set the stage for the first large soft-bodied organisms.

status_timeline.source: Hoffman et al. 1998, Science — repeated global bottlenecks and post-glacial recovery framed as an evolutionary filter
Neoproterozoic oxygenation debate, 2010s — the correlation is strong but the causal arrow between ice, oxygen and animals is still argued

claims.statement: Disc-shaped impressions in Flinders Ranges sandstone, described in 1947 as jellyfish, were the first Ediacarans found.
claims.asserted_by: Sprigg 1947, Transactions of the Royal Society of South Australia

status_timeline.source: Sprigg 1947, Trans. Roy. Soc. South Australia — 'Early Cambrian (?) jellyfishes'; the age was wrong and the paper was largely ignored
Glaessner and Wade, Adelaide, late 1950s — the fauna is recognised as genuinely Precambrian and becomes internationally known

claims.statement: The Ediacara fossils are Precambrian, not Cambrian: complex soft-bodied life predates the Cambrian explosion.
claims.asserted_by: Glaessner and colleagues, University of Adelaide, late 1950s (deliberately vague: the reassignment accrued over several papers)

status_timeline.source: Glaessner, Adelaide, 1959 — Ediacara fauna reassigned below the Cambrian; exact single citation deliberately not pinned
stratigraphic consensus, 1980s — a global Ediacaran assemblage is documented on five continents

claims.statement: The Ediacarans may be a failed experiment: quilted organisms unrelated to any animal phylum that survived.
claims.asserted_by: Seilacher 1992, Journal of the Geological Society (London)

status_timeline.source: Seilacher 1992, J. Geol. Soc. London — 'Vendobionta and Psammocorallia: lost constructions of Precambrian evolution'
Ediacaran affinity debate, ~2000 — rival readings place them as lichens, fungi, giant protists, or stem animals
Bobrovskiy et al. 2018, Science — cholesteroids show at least Dickinsonia was an animal, dissolving the strongest version of Vendobionta

claims.statement: Cholesterol biomarkers preserved in Dickinsonia show it was an animal, not a lichen, fungus or failed experiment.
claims.asserted_by: Bobrovskiy, Hope, Ivantsov, Nettersheim, Hallmann & Brocks 2018, Science

status_timeline.source: Bobrovskiy et al. 2018, Science — cholesteroids extracted from White Sea Dickinsonia films
Ediacaran palaeobiology, early 2020s — the animal affinity of Dickinsonia is now the majority position

claims.statement: In 2004 the Ediacaran became the first new geological period ratified in over a century, spanning 635 to 539 Ma.
claims.asserted_by: International Commission on Stratigraphy 2004 — ratification of the Ediacaran System

status_timeline.source: ICS 2004 — the golden spike is placed at the base of the Marinoan cap carbonate in Enorama Creek, South Australia
Knoll, Walter, Narbonne & Christie-Blick 2006, Lethaia — 'The Ediacaran Period: a new addition to the geologic time scale'

claims.statement: Almost every living animal phylum shows up in the fossil record within a geologic eyeblink, with no obvious ancestors below.
claims.asserted_by: Darwin 1859, On the Origin of Species

status_timeline.source: Darwin 1859, On the Origin of Species — flagged the abrupt Cambrian appearance as a serious objection to his own theory
Walcott 1911, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections — described the Burgess Shale fauna found in 1909, deepening rather than dissolving the puzzle
Erwin et al. 2011, Science — molecular clocks plus fossils framed the radiation as fast but not instantaneous

claims.statement: Zircon dating of Siberian sections puts the Cambrian base near 544 Ma and squeezes the main radiation into roughly 10 million years.

status_timeline.source: Bowring et al. 1993, Science — U-Pb ash dates from the Siberian Platform calibrated Early Cambrian evolution for the first time
Gradstein et al. 2004, A Geologic Time Scale 2004 — base of the Cambrian revised younger as new ash dates accumulated

claims.statement: The Cambrian begins 538.8 million years ago, about five million years later than the 1993 zircon calibration claimed.
claims.asserted_by: International Commission on Stratigraphy 2023, International Chronostratigraphic Chart

status_timeline.source: ICS 2023, International Chronostratigraphic Chart — anchored to the GSSP at Fortune Head, Newfoundland

claims.statement: Detrital zircons cap the Chengjiang fossil beds at 518.0 million years, fixing the radiation's showpiece deposit in absolute time.
claims.asserted_by: Yang et al. 2018, Journal of the Geological Society

status_timeline.source: Yang et al. 2018, J. Geol. Soc. — CA-ID-TIMS on detrital zircons gave a maximum age of 518.03 Ma for the Maotianshan Shale
Cambrian geochronology practice since about 2020 — the 518 Ma tie-point is now routinely cited; adoption date approximate

claims.statement: Some Burgess Shale animals are so strange that they may not fit inside any surviving phylum at all.
claims.asserted_by: Whittington 1975, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B

status_timeline.source: Whittington 1975, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B — redescription of Opabinia found no home for it among living groups
Gould 1989, Wonderful Life — popularised maximal Cambrian disparity and drew immediate pushback
Conway Morris 1998, The Crucible of Creation — argued most oddballs are stem members of known phyla
Phylogenetic consensus of the 2010s — cladistic restudies placed Opabinia and Hallucigenia on the stems of living groups

claims.statement: Two thumb-sized jawless fish from Chengjiang carry gill pouches and a notochord, making them the oldest known vertebrates.

status_timeline.source: Shu et al. 1999, Nature — Myllokunmingia and Haikouichthys described as Early Cambrian craniates
Shu et al. 2003, Nature — a larger specimen sample restated the head and backbone characters against sceptics
Conway Morris & Caron 2014, Nature — Metaspriggina from the Burgess Shale showed Cambrian vertebrates were real and widespread

claims.statement: The origin of vertebrates is one branch inside the Cambrian radiation, not a separate event with its own trigger.

status_timeline.source: Erwin et al. 2011, Science — the Cambrian conundrum framed as one radiation producing all bilaterian body plans

claims.statement: About 85% of marine species vanish at the end of the Ordovician, in the first of the Big Five mass extinctions.

status_timeline.source: Raup & Sepkoski 1982, Science — statistical analysis of marine families singled out five extinction peaks
Paleobiological consensus of the 1990s — the Big Five framework became standard in textbooks and compendia; date approximate
Stanley 2016, PNAS — reworked species-level magnitudes, keeping the end-Ordovician among the largest

claims.statement: A short, sharp Gondwanan ice age dropped sea level and chilled shelf seas, killing shallow-water life in two pulses.

status_timeline.source: Brenchley et al. 1994, Geology — oxygen and carbon isotopes plus the sea-level record pinned a brief glaciation in a greenhouse world
Finnegan et al. 2011, Science — clumped isotopes put tropical cooling and ice volume on a quantitative footing

claims.statement: Early moss-like plants weathering bare rock pulled down CO2 hard enough to help start the end-Ordovician glaciation.

status_timeline.source: Lenton et al. 2012, Nature Geoscience — weathering experiments with living mosses fed into a biogeochemical model
Earth-system modelling debate of the late 2010s — volcanic weathering and nutrient delivery remain competing drivers

claims.statement: Sporangia holding liverwort-like spores in Omani drill core show plants were already ashore by the Late Ordovician.

status_timeline.source: Wellman, Osterloff & Mohiuddin 2003, Nature — first sporangia with in situ cryptospores, from Katian rocks of Oman
Rubinstein et al. 2010, New Phytologist — Argentine cryptospores pushed the earliest evidence roughly 20 Myr older

claims.statement: Cryptospores from Argentina push the first land plants back to about 473 million years ago, into the Middle Ordovician.

status_timeline.source: Rubinstein et al. 2010, New Phytologist — Dapingian-Darriwilian cryptospores from the Central Andean Basin
Palynological consensus of the 2020s — a Middle Ordovician start is widely accepted, though the fossils are spores, not bodies

claims.statement: Scottish hot-spring chert froze a whole Early Devonian land ecosystem in silica, dated by zircon to 411.5 million years.
claims.asserted_by: Parry et al. 2011, Journal of the Geological Society

status_timeline.source: Parry et al. 2011, J. Geol. Soc. — U-Pb age of 411.5 +/- 1.1 Ma for the Rhynie cherts
Mark et al. 2011, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta — 40Ar/39Ar dating of the same hot-spring system gave a younger age
Rhynie geochronology debate, ongoing — radiometric ages and biostratigraphy have not fully converged; the date stays approximate

claims.statement: Tiktaalik, an Arctic Devonian fish with a neck and wrist bones inside its fins, sits squarely on the way to land.

status_timeline.source: Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins 2006, Nature — described from Late Devonian rocks of Ellesmere Island, Nunavut
Niedzwiedzki et al. 2010, Nature — Polish trackways dated far older complicated Tiktaalik's transitional position
Phylogenetic consensus of the 2010s-2020s — Tiktaalik remains a key stem tetrapod even if true tetrapods are older

claims.statement: Tetrapod trackways in a Polish quarry are 18 million years older than Tiktaalik, so four-legged walkers came first.

status_timeline.source: Niedzwiedzki et al. 2010, Nature — Eifelian trackways from Zachelmie quarry, Holy Cross Mountains
Devonian trace-fossil debate of the 2010s — some workers read the marks as fish feeding traces or inorganic; interpretation still argued

claims.statement: Ichthyostega from East Greenland has real limbs with digits but still a fish's tail fin and gill skeleton.

status_timeline.source: Save-Soderbergh 1932, Meddelelser om Gronland — named from Danish expedition material as the earliest known tetrapod
Coates & Clack 1990, Nature — polydactylous limbs showed the five-digit pattern was not original, reframing the fish-to-tetrapod transition

claims.statement: Vast everwet swamp forests of tree-sized lycopsids buried so much carbon that they became the world's main coal seams.

status_timeline.source: Coal-measures paleobotany, mid-19th century — the plant origin of coal was settled well before 1850; the knowledge date here is approximate
Dawson 1868, Acadian Geology — upright fossil trees at Joggins showed the swamp forests were buried where they grew

claims.statement: Burying that much undecayed plant carbon drove atmospheric oxygen toward 35%, the highest level of the last 600 million years.
claims.asserted_by: Berner & Canfield 1989, American Journal of Science

status_timeline.source: Berner & Canfield 1989, Am. J. Sci. — a carbon and sulfur mass-balance model produced a late Paleozoic oxygen peak
Berner 2006, Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta — the GEOCARBSULF model retained the late Paleozoic oxygen high
Model-dependence debate of the 2010s — the absolute peak value varies widely between models, though a high is robust

claims.statement: Coal piled up because plants invented lignin before fungi learned to rot it, so dead wood simply did not decay.

status_timeline.source: Robinson 1990, Geology — argued lignin-degrading organisms were rare or absent through the Paleozoic
Floudas et al. 2012, Science — 31 fungal genomes dated white-rot lignin peroxidases to near the Carboniferous-Permian boundary
Nelsen et al. 2016, PNAS — lignin was secondary in many coal floras; everwet tropics and Pangean basins now favoured instead

claims.statement: The Great Dying wiped out roughly 81% of marine species, the closest life has come to being switched off entirely.

status_timeline.source: Raup 1979, Science — rarefaction of marine genera implied a bottleneck of up to 96% of species lost
Bowring et al. 1998, Science — showed the main killing pulse lasted well under a million years
Stanley 2016, PNAS — revised the marine loss down to about 81% of species using a corrected estimator

claims.statement: Pre-zircon timescales placed the Permian-Triassic boundary near 250 million years, give or take about ten million.
claims.asserted_by: Harland et al. 1982, A Geologic Time Scale (Cambridge University Press)

status_timeline.source: Harland et al. 1982, A Geologic Time Scale — best available interpolation from sparse and mostly imprecise radiometric anchors
Bowring et al. 1998, Science — U-Pb zircon dating from South China gave 251.4 +/- 0.3 Ma, cutting the error by an order of magnitude

claims.statement: The boundary falls at 251.902 million years ago, and the extinction itself took only about 60,000 years.

status_timeline.source: Burgess, Bowring & Shen 2014, PNAS — five ash beds at the Meishan GSSP dated by CA-ID-TIMS U-Pb on zircon
International Chronostratigraphic Chart, since the late 2010s — 251.902 +/- 0.024 Ma adopted as the boundary age

claims.statement: Millions of cubic kilometres of basalt flooded Siberia in under a million years, one of the largest eruptions ever.

status_timeline.source: Renne & Basu 1991, Science — 40Ar/39Ar laser dating gave an eruption duration of 0.9 +/- 0.8 Myr
Burgess & Bowring 2015, Science Advances — U-Pb dating confirmed the volume and compressed the timeline further

claims.statement: Flaked-looking stones in a high Mexican cave are claimed as tools from 26,500 years ago; most archaeologists doubt it.
claims.asserted_by: Ardelean et al. 2020, Nature — Evidence of human occupation in Mexico around the Last Glacial Maximum

status_timeline.source: Ardelean et al. 2020, Nature — ~1,900 stone objects, no hearths and no human DNA; exact coordinates withheld
Chatters et al. 2022, PaleoAmerica — argues the objects are geofacts from natural rockfall

claims.statement: The ice-free corridor was biologically dead until roughly 12,600 years ago, so the first people must have come by coast.
claims.asserted_by: Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature — Postglacial viability and colonization in North America's ice-free corridor

status_timeline.source: Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature — sedimentary ancient DNA shows the corridor lacked forage until ~12.6 ka
the Pacific coastal route is now the default entry model in review literature

claims.statement: Wheat, barley, sheep and goats were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent between about 11,700 and 9,500 years ago.
claims.asserted_by: Zeder 2011, Current Anthropology — The Origins of Agriculture in the Near East

status_timeline.source: Childe 1936, Man Makes Himself — the 'Neolithic Revolution' framed as a single oasis-driven event
Braidwood's Jarmo excavations relocate origins to the hilly flanks of the Zagros and Taurus
Zeder 2011 — domestication reframed as a slow, multi-site process rather than a revolution

claims.statement: Hunter-gatherers raised carved megalithic enclosures at Gobekli Tepe before any crop was domesticated nearby.
claims.asserted_by: Schmidt 2000, Paleorient — Gobekli Tepe, Southeastern Turkey: A Preliminary Report on the 1995-1999 Excavations

status_timeline.source: Schmidt 2000, Paleorient — monumental construction by foragers inverts the usual causal story
debate over whether ritual aggregation drove farming, or merely coincided with it
the pre-agricultural age of the enclosures is accepted; the causal claim is not

claims.statement: Farming was invented at least seven times independently, in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and elsewhere.
claims.asserted_by: Diamond & Bellwood 2003, Science — Farmers and Their Languages: The First Expansions

status_timeline.source: Harlan 1971, Science — 'centres and non-centres' breaks the single-hearth model of agriculture
Diamond & Bellwood 2003, Science — multiple independent origins treated as settled

claims.statement: The first writing is an accountant's script: pictographic ration tablets pressed into clay at Uruk around 3300 BCE.
claims.asserted_by: Nissen, Damerow & Englund 1993, Archaic Bookkeeping (University of Chicago Press)

status_timeline.source: Falkenstein 1936, Archaische Texte aus Uruk — the archaic tablet corpus published from Uruk IV
Nissen et al. 1993 — the archaic texts shown to be almost entirely administrative accounts

claims.statement: Cuneiform grew out of clay counting tokens sealed in envelopes: the marks on the outside became the script.
claims.asserted_by: Schmandt-Besserat 1992, Before Writing (University of Texas Press)

status_timeline.source: Schmandt-Besserat 1978, Scientific American — the token-to-sign hypothesis
Schmandt-Besserat 1992 — widely cited, but critics dispute how many signs really derive from tokens

claims.statement: Alloying copper with about a tenth part tin gave a harder metal, and forced the first long-distance trade in ore.
claims.asserted_by: Thomsen's three-age system, 1836, Ledetraad til Nordisk Oldkyndighed; refined by 20th-century metallurgical analysis

status_timeline.source: Thomsen 1836 — stone, bronze and iron as successive ages of material culture
trace-element and lead-isotope work on artifacts confirms tin bronze and its distant ore sources

claims.statement: An olive branch buried alive by Theran pumice radiocarbon-dates the eruption to between 1627 and 1600 BCE.
claims.asserted_by: Friedrich et al. 2006, Science — Santorini Eruption Radiocarbon Dated to 1627-1600 B.C.

status_timeline.source: Friedrich et al. 2006, Science — wiggle-matched radiocarbon on an olive branch from Phira quarry
Manning et al. 2006, Science — independent radiocarbon series supports the high chronology; Aegean archaeologists object
still unresolved against the Egyptian-synchronism date; no accepted reconciliation

claims.statement: Pottery synchronisms with dated Egyptian reigns place the Thera eruption a century later, near 1500 BCE.
claims.asserted_by: Warren & Hankey 1989, Aegean Bronze Age Chronology (Bristol Classical Press)

status_timeline.source: Warren & Hankey 1989 — the low chronology, anchored to Egyptian king-lists, is the archaeological default
radiocarbon results push the eruption a century earlier; the ceramic synchronisms are defended, not abandoned

claims.statement: Olive trees do not reliably lay down annual rings, so the olive-branch date may be more precise than it is accurate.
claims.asserted_by: Cherubini et al. 2014, Antiquity — Bronze Age catastrophe and modern controversy: dating the Santorini eruption

status_timeline.source: Cherubini et al. 2014, Antiquity — questions the ring counts underlying the wiggle-match
Friedrich and Manning reply that the chronology stands irrespective of ring counting

claims.statement: Within about fifty years around 1200 BCE nearly every palace state of the eastern Mediterranean burned or was abandoned.
claims.asserted_by: Drews 1993, The End of the Bronze Age (Princeton University Press)

status_timeline.source: Egyptological reading of the Medinet Habu 'Sea Peoples' reliefs as a record of general catastrophe
Drews 1993 — the simultaneity of the destruction layers is accepted; the cause is not

claims.statement: The Thera eruption destroyed Minoan sea power and set off the wider Bronze Age collapse.
claims.asserted_by: Marinatos 1939, Antiquity — The Volcanic Destruction of Minoan Crete

status_timeline.source: Marinatos 1939, Antiquity — ash and tsunami invoked to explain the Cretan destruction horizons
Cretan palaces shown to fall generations after the eruption, not with it
radiocarbon opens a gap of three to four centuries between eruption and collapse

claims.statement: No single cause fits: drought, earthquake, migration and the brittleness of palace trade networks acted together.
claims.asserted_by: Cline 2014, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (Princeton University Press)

status_timeline.source: Cline 2014 — systems-collapse framing drawing on pollen and speleothem drought proxies
multicausal systems collapse is now the standard account in the literature

claims.statement: Harold Godwinson's shield wall broke on Senlac Hill on 14 October 1066 — a date known to the day.
claims.asserted_by: Freeman 1867, The History of the Norman Conquest of England, drawing on the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle

status_timeline.source: Freeman 1867 — contemporary annals converge on the day; the site at Battle Abbey is the only live question

claims.statement: Gutenberg's Mainz workshop combined a cast type alloy, oil ink and a screw press around 1440.
claims.asserted_by: bibliographic consensus on Gutenberg's Mainz workshop, 19th-20th century; the 1455 Helmasperger instrument is the firm anchor

status_timeline.source: the 1455 notarial record fixes the enterprise; the ~1440 start date remains an inference, hence the +/- 5 years

claims.statement: Cheap print made technical knowledge cumulative and comparable, a precondition for industrial mechanisation.
claims.asserted_by: Eisenstein 1979, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (Cambridge University Press)

status_timeline.source: Eisenstein 1979 — print fixity and standardisation as an engine of the scientific and industrial revolutions
Johns 1998, The Nature of the Book — argues print was unreliable and 'fixity' was a later achievement

claims.statement: Between roughly 1760 and 1840 Britain moved from muscle and water to coal-fired steam, and never went back.
claims.asserted_by: Toynbee 1884, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England

status_timeline.source: Toynbee 1884 — names and periodises the Industrial Revolution as 1760-1840
the periodisation becomes standard in economic history
Crafts 1985, British Economic Growth during the Industrial Revolution — growth was slower and more gradual than the label implies

claims.statement: Tambora erupted on 10 April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history, and lost 1,400 metres of its own summit.
claims.asserted_by: Stothers 1984, Science — The Great Tambora Eruption in 1815 and Its Aftermath

status_timeline.source: Raffles' contemporary eyewitness reports from Java fix the date and scale
Stothers 1984, Science — quantifies the eruption and its atmospheric aftermath

claims.statement: 1816 had no summer in New England and Europe: June snow, failed harvests, and the worst famine of the century.
claims.asserted_by: Stommel & Stommel 1979, Scientific American — The Year Without a Summer

status_timeline.source: Stommel & Stommel 1979 — reconstructs the 1816 cold anomaly from diaries and harvest records
the anomaly is confirmed by instrumental and proxy climate reconstructions

claims.statement: Tambora's sulfate veil dimmed the northern hemisphere by roughly half a degree, causing the 1816 crop failures.
claims.asserted_by: Oppenheimer 2003, Progress in Physical Geography — Climatic, environmental and human consequences of Tambora 1815

status_timeline.source: Humphreys 1913 — volcanic dust proposed as a cause of historical cold years
ice-core sulfate spikes tie the 1816 anomaly to the 1815 eruption
Oppenheimer 2003 — synthesises the forcing, the cooling and the human toll

claims.statement: At 05:29 on 16 July 1945 a plutonium device fired in the New Mexico desert and fused the sand into green glass.
claims.asserted_by: Manhattan Project records, declassified 1945 (Smyth Report, Atomic Energy for Military Purposes)

status_timeline.source: Smyth Report 1945 — the test is public record within weeks; trinitite is its physical trace

claims.statement: Fallout plutonium and carbon-14 from 1950s bomb tests are a sharp, global, permanent layer in the world's sediments.
claims.asserted_by: Waters et al. 2015, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists — Can nuclear weapons fallout mark the beginning of the Anthropocene epoch?

status_timeline.source: Waters et al. 2015 — the bomb spike put forward as the sharpest available global stratigraphic marker
the marker's reality is not disputed even by those who reject the epoch

claims.statement: Humanity has become a geological force, and the epoch we live in should be renamed the Anthropocene.

status_timeline.source: Crutzen & Stoermer 2000, IGBP Newsletter — the term coined, with an informal 1800 CE start
Crutzen 2002, Nature — 'Geology of mankind' brings the term to a general scientific audience
the ICS convenes an Anthropocene Working Group to test the concept formally
rejected as a formal epoch but retained in wide informal use across the earth and social sciences

claims.statement: The Anthropocene should begin in 1952, with a golden spike in the varved mud of Crawford Lake, Ontario.
claims.asserted_by: McCarthy et al. 2023, The Anthropocene Review — the varved succession of Crawford Lake as a candidate GSSP

status_timeline.source: AWG names Crawford Lake the GSSP candidate in July 2023; formal proposal submitted 31 October 2023
March 2024 — the ICS Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy votes it down, 12 of 18 against

claims.statement: The 2024 vote that killed the Anthropocene was itself attacked as procedurally irregular before being upheld.
claims.asserted_by: public commentary following the March 2024 SQS vote, including Oreskes' 'sham' remark; IUGS subsequently affirmed the process

status_timeline.source: AWG members and outside historians allege irregularities; the IUGS confirms the vote followed its statutes

claims.statement: Human interference with climate began 8,000 years ago with forest clearance and rice paddies, not in 1952.
claims.asserted_by: Ruddiman 2003, Climatic Change — The anthropogenic greenhouse era began thousands of years ago

status_timeline.source: Ruddiman 2003 — anomalous Holocene CO2 and CH4 attributed to early farming
critics argue the early emissions are far too small; the hypothesis remains a live minority position

claims.statement: Burning fossil carbon at industrial scale is what made humans a planetary force, so the Anthropocene starts around 1800.
claims.asserted_by: Steffen, Crutzen & McNeill 2007, Ambio — The Anthropocene: Are Humans Now Overwhelming the Great Forces of Nature?

status_timeline.source: Steffen et al. 2007, Ambio — Stage 1 of the Anthropocene dated to the industrial era
the AWG shifts to a 1950s 'Great Acceleration' start with a sharper stratigraphic signal
with no formal epoch, the industrial start date survives as one informal usage among several

claims.statement: Rock layers were laid down in sequence, the lowest first, so strata record an order of events.
claims.asserted_by: Steno 1669, De solido intra solidum naturaliter contento prodromus

status_timeline.source: Steno 1669, Florence — superposition, original horizontality and lateral continuity, from dissecting Tuscan hillsides
stratigraphic practice, c. 1800 — superposition becomes the working assumption of field geology

claims.statement: The rock cycle has run so long that the record shows no vestige of a beginning and no prospect of an end.
claims.asserted_by: Hutton 1788, Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh

status_timeline.source: Hutton 1788 — the angular unconformity at Siccar Point read as two complete cycles of deposition, uplift and erosion
scriptural geology, c. 1800 — an indefinitely old Earth is resisted on theological grounds
geological consensus, c. 1840 — an Earth vastly older than human record is taken as established

claims.statement: Present-day rates of erosion and deposition are enough to explain the past; no former catastrophes need be invoked.

status_timeline.source: Lyell 1830-1833 — Hutton's deep time restated as strict uniformity of rate as well as of process
geological consensus, c. 1860 — uniformitarianism becomes the disciplinary default
Alvarez et al. 1980, Science — a sudden extraterrestrial catastrophe reopens the question of rate

claims.statement: The Earth's heat loss limits its age to somewhere between twenty and four hundred million years, most likely about a hundred.
claims.asserted_by: Thomson (Kelvin) 1862, Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh

status_timeline.source: Thomson 1862, On the Secular Cooling of the Earth — a cooling sphere with no internal heat source
physical consensus, 1870s-1890s — Kelvin's authority compresses the geological timescale against the objections of geologists and of Darwin
Curie & Laborde 1903, Comptes Rendus — radium generates heat, so the Earth is not a simply cooling body
Holmes 1913, The Age of the Earth — radiometric ages exceed Kelvin's ceiling outright

claims.statement: Lead accumulating in uranium minerals gives rock ages from four hundred million up to two thousand million years.

status_timeline.source: Boltwood 1907 — the first uranium-lead ages, on ten mineral samples
age-of-the-Earth debate, 1920s — radiometric ages accepted in principle, the numbers still moving
Patterson 1956 — the meteoritic lead isochron settles the figure near 4.55 Ga

claims.statement: Radioactive decay makes the Earth at least sixteen hundred million years old, far beyond any cooling estimate.
claims.asserted_by: Holmes 1913, The Age of the Earth (Harper & Brothers)

status_timeline.source: Holmes 1913 — the first sustained argument for a radiometric geological timescale
National Research Council report on the age of the Earth, 1931 — radiometric dating formally endorsed
Patterson 1956 — superseded by the meteoritic lead isochron

claims.statement: Matching Carboniferous floras and glacial beds on now-separate continents mean the landmasses were once joined.
claims.asserted_by: Wegener 1915, Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane

status_timeline.source: Wegener 1915 — Pangaea argued from the fit of coastlines and the distribution of the Glossopteris flora
American Association of Petroleum Geologists symposium, 1926-1928 — drift rejected, largely for lacking a mechanism
Vine & Matthews 1963, Nature — magnetic striping on the seafloor supplies the missing mechanism
Morgan 1968 and Le Pichon 1968 — plate tectonics becomes the framework of the earth sciences

claims.statement: The Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary sits at sixty-five million years, the round figure carried by textbooks for decades.
claims.asserted_by: Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary age, textbook consensus c. 1980-2005 (no single originating paper)

status_timeline.source: timescale consensus, 1980s-1990s — deliberately vague attribution; 65 Ma was a rounded figure in general circulation, not one group's result
Renne et al. 2013, Science — recalibration moves the boundary to 66.043 Ma and the round number retires

claims.statement: Argon dating of boundary tektites and ash puts the extinction at 66.043 million years, to within eleven thousand.

status_timeline.source: Renne et al. 2013, Science — Time Scales of Critical Events Around the Cretaceous-Paleogene Boundary
geochronological consensus, mid-2010s — 66.0 Ma adopted by the international timescale

claims.statement: The second great freeze, the Marinoan, ends at 635 million years, the boundary that now opens the Ediacaran.

status_timeline.source: Condon et al. 2005, Science — U-Pb ages from the Doushantuo Formation, South China
chronostratigraphic consensus — 635 Ma ratified as the base of the Ediacaran, at the top of the Marinoan cap carbonate
